# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
This is a strong follow-up. It answers most of the open questions from the earlier documents:
- **Durability.** It provides the first controlled evidence on how long the gain lasts.
- **Meeting baseline.** It reports baseline meeting data, which removes my earlier concern that the treated–control difference in meeting time might have existed before the trial.
- **Unclaimed work.** It adds a second hours measure, independent of timesheets, to check for unclaimed work.
- **Earlier claims.** It tests the Varga comment and the meta-analysis fairly. Its finding that the four long-follow-up studies in the meta-analysis were all uncontrolled and used scheduled hours confirms the weakness I flagged in that review's "no decay" claim.

The arithmetic checks out:
- Varden, timesheets: 0.966 / 0.88 → +9.8%.
- Varden, logs: 0.966 / 0.89 → +8.5%.
- Halden survivors: 96.8 / 86.6 → +11.8%, with hours 34.9 / 40.3 → −13.4%.

The main issues are below.

## 1. Control offices also cut meetings, which affects the decline estimate

Two of the seven control offices ran a meeting audit at month 15, and their output per hour then rose 4.1%. The paper treats this as a side observation, but it changes the comparison group:
- **The control average moved up.** If offices are of similar size, two offices gaining about 4% raise the control average by about 1.2 points. That is a sizeable share of the 2.7-point fall from 12.5% to 9.8%. Part of the measured "fading" may therefore be the control group improving, not the treatment effect weakening. The 24-month gap understates the effect of the reduced schedule itself.
- **Report it both ways.** The 24-month results should be shown with and without those two offices, or with their post-month-15 data handled separately. The paper should also say whether the audit was prompted by knowledge of the treated offices, which would make it spillover.
- **The control meeting figures need reconciling.** If the two audit offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours, the overall control average should drop by about 0.6 hours. The reported drop is only 7.2 → 7.0. That implies meeting time rose by about 0.5 hours in the other five control offices. The figures may be correct, but the paper should state this.

The audit is also interesting in its own right. Applying the 47% meetings share to the 8.5% gain gives about 4.0 points from a 3.5-hour cut in treated offices. The audit offices gained 4.1% from a 2.1-hour cut. With only two offices and no controls this proves little, but it supports the paper's suggestion that part of the gain may be achievable without cutting hours. A trial arm that cuts meetings but keeps hours unchanged is the obvious next step, and the paper could say so.

## 2. The mediation result is weaker than "confirms" suggests

- **Same offices that suggested the hypothesis.** The registered test is a confirmatory analysis in the same seven treated offices whose month-6 data suggested it. Registering before the 24-month outcomes is good practice, but this is not independent replication. "Survives a registered test" is accurate. "Confirms", in the Summary, is too strong.
- **Effective sample size.** The paper cites "a larger sample of office-months", but the trial randomised 14 offices. Repeated months from the same office are correlated. An interval of 28–66% for a proportion mediated looks narrow for 14 clusters. The paper should say how the confidence interval was computed and whether it accounts for clustering, for example with a cluster bootstrap.
- **Causal assumptions.** Neither meeting time nor fatigue was randomised. Mediation estimates assume no confounding between mediator and outcome; the Limitations section acknowledges this, but the Summary does not.
- **Interacting pathways.** The shares (47 + 18 + 35 = 100) treat the two pathways as additive. Fewer meetings could plausibly reduce fatigue, so the pathways may overlap. The paper should state how this was handled.

## 3. What do the system logs actually measure?

The logs are described as recording "time staff are working on cases". If they capture only time on the case-management system, meetings are excluded. Then the numbers don't fit:
- Baseline: 37.9 timesheet hours minus 7.4 hours of meetings leaves about 30.5 hours of case time.
- Month 24: about 33.4 timesheet hours minus 3.9 hours of meetings leaves about 29.5 hours of case time.

On that reading, log hours should fall by only about 3%, not 11%. The per-hour gain on the log measure would then be much smaller.

The −11% figure makes sense only if the logs measure total logged-in time, including meetings. The paper needs to define the measure precisely, because the two readings imply very different things:
- **If the logs exclude meetings**, the meetings pathway works through output per hour of case work, for example fewer interruptions. That would be a stronger mechanism claim.
- **If the logs include meetings**, part of the meetings effect is an accounting effect: the same hours with less meeting time leave more time for cases. That is still useful, but it is a different kind of finding.

Also note that the logs miss work done outside the system, such as phone calls, email and paper files.

## 4. The Halden subset

- **The marketing agency doesn't fit the coverage story.** The Summary says all three reverting organisations had "client-facing or coverage obligations". A marketing agency facing client deadlines is discretionary, deadline-driven work under the meta-analysis's classification, not coverage-bound work. It is a discretionary organisation that reverted, and the Summary should say so rather than fold it into the coverage explanation.
- **"Upper bound" is too strong.** These are two-year before–after figures with no comparison group. They include whatever happened to productivity generally over 2023–25, including the spread of AI tools in knowledge work, and that trend could run in either direction. "Likely overstates" is safer.
- **Include the reverters.** An estimate covering all 14 organisations, counting the three that reverted, would help. Their output indices of 88–91 at reversion are exactly the outcomes that a survivors-only estimate leaves out.
- **Non-response.** Nine of the 23 organisations contacted didn't respond. The paper should say whether they differ from the 14 on their pilot-period outcomes.
- **Check the baseline figure.** The baseline of 40.3 hours is identical to the Varga comment's figure for a different subset of 27 organisations. It may be a coincidence, but it's worth checking for a copy error.

## 5. The counter arm

- **The cost estimate needs explaining.** 12% more staff raising cost per contact by 9% is consistent if labour is about 75% of costs, but the paper should state that. Otherwise readers will expect +12%.
- **Report the full month-12 results.** These should include output per FTE and per hour, not just waiting times. The waiting-time comparison is now treated vs control (7.3 vs 4.0 minutes), which is an improvement on the nine-month report's before–after figure.

## 6. Smaller points

- **Few clusters.** With 7 v 7 offices, conventional clustered confidence intervals tend to be too narrow, as I noted on the nine-month report. Use wild cluster bootstrap or randomisation inference.
- **The decline isn't statistically established.** The 9- and 24-month confidence intervals overlap heavily. A paired test of the change within the same offices would show whether the decline is distinguishable from zero. Taken together with §1, "consistent with some fading" is about as far as the data go.
- **"About a quarter" mixes two comparisons.** On the like-for-like timesheet measure, 12.5% → 9.8% is a fall of about 22%. From 12.5% to the log-based 8.5% it is about 32%. Say which is meant.
- **Cost per case is still missing.** With output per FTE at −3.4%, full pay and some paid overtime, cost per case has risen. The paper should report it, and say whether the county has decided to keep the reduced schedule in case-processing.
- **Rebuttal of the Varga comment.** The comment's prediction concerned self-reported energy returning to baseline. The paper's restatement, that the gain would fall to zero by month ten, is the inference the comment drew from that, so it is fair. Note also that fatigue still shows +0.34 SD at 24 months, which directly contradicts the energy-decay argument.
- **Authors testing their own claims.** The original authors are testing their own hypothesis, and in Okafor's case their own pilot. Registration largely addresses this, but a sentence acknowledging it would help.

## Overall

The central conclusions are well supported:
- A per-hour gain of roughly 8–10% persists at 24 months in randomised, record-based, log-measured data.
- Coverage-bound work could not sustain the change.
- The long-follow-up evidence in the meta-analysis could not speak to decay.

Before publication, the paper should:
- account for the control-office meeting audit when estimating decline;
- define what the system logs measure;
- explain how the mediation confidence interval handles clustering, and soften "confirms";
- describe the marketing-agency reversion accurately.

I can draft a referee report from these notes, or write a short synthesis of what the five documents together establish and what remains open.
